A mugwump is a person who refuses to commit to one political side — someone who stays deliberately independent, switches allegiances, or simply refuses to pledge loyalty to any group.

The word became famous during the 1884 U.S. presidential election. A group of Republicans couldn't bring themselves to vote for their own party's candidate, James G. Blaine, whom they viewed as corrupt. So they crossed over and voted for the Democrat, Grover Cleveland instead. These party-defectors were branded "mugwumps." They believed their personal conscience was more important than blind party loyalty.

From that event, the word expanded into everyday use in two directions:

1. A political fence-sitter. Someone who refuses to take a clear stance, hovering in the middle without committing to either side. This is the meaning you'll encounter most often. There's a famous old joke: "A mugwump is a bird that sits on the fence with its mug on one side and its wump on the other." In other words, its face points one way, its rear points the other — the creature is perfectly, ridiculously stuck in the middle.

2. A self-important person, a "big shot." Someone who acts as though they hold great authority or importance — a pompous little ruler of their own small world. This meaning is more common in British English. If someone on a neighbourhood committee acts like a grand emperor handing down edicts, you might call them the mugwump of that committee.
Is it an insult or a compliment?

Almost always, it carries a mocking or critical edge.

  • In the fence-sitter sense, calling someone a mugwump suggests they are indecisive, spineless, or too cowardly to commit. Taking a real stand requires courage; a mugwump dodges that.
  • In the big shot sense, it implies the person has an inflated view of their own importance that others don't necessarily share — it's gentle ridicule.

Very rarely, someone might wear the label with pride, as the original 1884 Republicans eventually did, implying they're too principled to be tied down by party machinery. But in everyday use, it's rarely a compliment.

The word has an old-fashioned, slightly literary or humorous flavour. It's not something you'd hear in casual daily conversation. You're more likely to come across it in:

  • Political journalism or commentary, especially around independent or bipartisan politicians
  • Historical writing about 19th-century American politics
  • British English, where it has had a longer shelf life — notably, Prime Minister Boris Johnson called a political opponent a "mutton-headed old mugwump" in 2017, which briefly brought the word back into headlines
  • Humour and satire, where its comical sound does half the work for you

• "Don't be such a mugwump — pick a side and defend it."
  • "He considered himself the mugwump of the office, dispensing opinions as though they were royal decrees."
  • "Her mugwump tendencies frustrated both parties; she consistently voted with neither."

In short: Call someone a mugwump and you're saying they either refuse to commit to any side (the fence-sitter), or they're walking around with an exaggerated sense of their own importance (the big shot). The first meaning is the sharper and more lasting one.
